definition: The shape of a signal plotted against time, usually over one cycle: for example sine, sawtooth, square or triangle. Two notes at the same pitch with different waveforms sound different.
example: A sawtooth waveform ramps up steadily and then drops straight back down, once per cycle.

definition: How far a wave swings from its centre line: a pressure difference in air, volts in a circuit, or a number (conventionally up to 1.0) in software. Bigger amplitude generally sounds louder.
example: A sine with amplitude 0.5 swings between −0.5 and +0.5.

definition: The time one complete cycle of a repeating wave takes, in seconds. It is one divided by the frequency.
example: A 440 Hz tone has a period of 1/440 s, about 2.27 ms.

definition: How many complete cycles something repeating makes per second, such as a sound wave or a processor clock, measured in hertz (Hz). It is one divided by the period.
example: Concert A is a frequency of 440 Hz: 440 cycles every second.

definition: The SI unit of frequency: one cycle per second. A kilohertz (kHz) is 1,000 Hz and a megahertz (MHz) is 1,000,000 Hz. Sample rates are also quoted in hertz (samples per second).
example: Human hearing spans roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz; audio is commonly sampled at 48 kHz.

definition: The distance one cycle of a wave occupies as it travels through a medium such as air, in metres. It equals the speed of sound divided by the frequency. It matters for acoustics and speakers, not for the numbers inside a synth.
example: In air at 20 °C a 100 Hz tone has a wavelength of about 3.43 m.

definition: The Greek letter λ (lambda), the usual symbol for wavelength in formulas such as λ = c / f.
example: For 440 Hz in air, λ ≈ 343 / 440 ≈ 0.78 m.

definition: How fast sound travels through a medium. In dry air at 20 °C it is about 343 metres per second; it rises with temperature and is much higher in water or solids.
example: Sound takes about 2.9 ms to travel 1 m in air.

definition: The SI unit of speed: how many metres something travels each second.
example: The speed of sound in air at 20 °C is about 343 m/s.

definition: The background pressure of the air around us, about 101,325 pascals at sea level. Sound is a tiny, rapid rise and fall of pressure around this value.
example: Even a very loud sound changes the pressure by only a small fraction of atmospheric pressure.

definition: The stiff, usually cone-shaped diaphragm of a loudspeaker driver. It moves back and forth with the signal and pushes the air to make sound.
example: A woofer cone moving in and out 100 times a second produces a 100 Hz tone.

definition: The SI unit of electric potential difference (voltage), the "pressure" that pushes current through a circuit. Audio signals in a circuit are voltages that rise and fall with the sound.
example: A pro line-level signal at +4 dBu is about 1.23 V RMS.

definition: The SI unit of time, symbol s. Audio work often uses milliseconds (ms, thousandths) and microseconds (µs, millionths) of a second.
example: One sample at 48 kHz lasts 1/48,000 s, about 20.8 µs.

definition: One thousandth of a second. Audio block durations and latencies are usually quoted in milliseconds.
example: A 48-sample block at 48 kHz lasts 1 ms.

definition: One millionth of a second.
example: Samples at 48 kHz are about 20.8 µs apart.

definition: The span of frequencies people can hear, usually quoted as roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz. The upper limit falls with age, and the figures are a rule of thumb rather than hard limits.
example: Audio sample rates (44.1 and 48 kHz) are chosen so that half the rate sits just above 20 kHz.

definition: The tendency of a system (a room, a string, a filter) to respond much more strongly at particular frequencies. In a synth filter, "resonance" is a control that boosts frequencies near the cut-off.
example: Turning up a resonant low-pass filter makes it whistle at its cut-off frequency.

definition: Where in its cycle a wave is at a given moment, measured as a fraction of a cycle (0 to 1), in degrees (0° to 360°) or in radians (0 to 2π). Phase matters when waves are combined and when it jumps suddenly.
example: A quarter of a cycle is a phase of 0.25, 90° or π/2 radians.

definition: Two identical waves are in phase when their peaks line up, so they add to double the amplitude. Half a cycle (180°) out of phase, one is the negative of the other and they cancel to silence.
example: Two equal sines in phase give +6 dB; the same pair 180° out of phase gives nothing.

definition: A sudden change in a wave's phase in the middle of a tone, which makes the waveform leap to a new value between two samples. It is usually heard as a click.
example: Switching a sine from 440 Hz to 450 Hz by recomputing it from absolute time can make the output leap from 0 to full scale in one sample.

definition: An instant jump in a waveform's value, such as the drop at the end of each sawtooth cycle. A discontinuity contains energy at very many frequencies, so it is heard as a click and causes aliasing in naive digital oscillators.
example: A square wave has two discontinuities per cycle.

definition: The unit of angle used by maths libraries. One radian is the angle at which the arc of a circle equals its radius; a full cycle is 2π radians (about 6.283), the same as 360°.
example: Python's math.sin(math.pi / 2) is 1.0 because π/2 radians is 90°.

definition: The unit of angular frequency: how many radians a phase turns through each second. Multiply a frequency in hertz by 2π to get it.
example: 440 Hz is about 2764.6 rad/s.

definition: A circle of radius 1. Walking once round it covers a distance of 2π, which is why one full cycle of a wave is 2π radians.
example: A quarter of the way round the unit circle is π/2 radians.

definition: The constant π, the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, about 3.14159. In audio formulas 2π converts cycles into radians.
example: One full cycle of a sine is 2π ≈ 6.283 radians.

definition: The Greek letter φ (phi). In the sine formula it is the starting phase in radians: where in the cycle the wave is at time zero.
example: A starting phase φ of π/2 turns a sine into a cosine.

definition: The Greek letter θ (theta), commonly used for an angle or a phase in radians.
example: sin(θ + π) = −sin(θ): half a cycle on, a sine has the opposite value.

definition: Frequency measured in radians per second instead of cycles per second, written ω (omega). It equals 2π times the frequency in hertz.
The smooth, purest periodic wave, following the sine function. It contains exactly one frequency, and every other periodic sound can be built by adding sines together.
example: A 440 Hz sine wave sounds like a plain, flute-like A.

definition: The trigonometric function that turns an angle into a value between −1 and +1, repeating every 2π radians. Most programming languages' sin takes radians, not degrees.
example: sin(π/2) = 1, but Python's math.sin(90) is about 0.894 because 90 is read as radians.

definition: The trigonometric function that is the sine shifted a quarter cycle earlier: cos(θ) = sin(θ + π/2). A cosine wave is a sine wave with a starting phase of 90°.
example: cos(0) = 1, while sin(0) = 0.

definition: A smooth S-shaped mathematical function that is almost a straight line near zero and flattens out towards −1 and +1 for large inputs. It is a common soft-clipping curve.

A sine component of a sound at a whole-number multiple of its fundamental frequency. The 1st harmonic is the fundamental, the 2nd is twice its frequency, and so on. Measurements label them H2, H3, … for the 2nd, 3rd, … harmonic.
example: A 220 Hz sawtooth has harmonics at 440, 660, 880 Hz and upwards.

definition: Harmonics at odd multiples of the fundamental (1st, 3rd, 5th, …). Square waves and symmetric clipping contain only odd harmonics; even harmonics (2nd, 4th, …) come from waveforms without half-wave symmetry, such as asymmetrically clipped ones.
example: A 5 kHz sine clipped symmetrically gains harmonics at 15, 25, 35 kHz and so on.

definition: The lowest frequency in a periodic sound: the rate at which the whole waveform repeats. It usually sets the pitch we hear.
example: A sawtooth with harmonics at 110, 220, 330 Hz … has a fundamental of 110 Hz.

definition: The set of frequencies at every whole-number multiple of a fundamental (1×, 2×, 3×, …). Its lower members give the octave, fifth and major third that musical tuning is built on. In maths the same name is used for the sum 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + …, which grows like a logarithm.
example: The harmonic series of 110 Hz is 110, 220, 330, 440, 550 Hz and so on.

definition: In audio, the position of a harmonic in the harmonic series: the whole number n by which the fundamental frequency is multiplied to give that harmonic's frequency. The fundamental is harmonic number 1. (In maths, 'harmonic number' means something else: the sum 1 + 1/2 + … + 1/n.)
example: With a 200 Hz fundamental, the 600 Hz component has harmonic number 600 / 200 = 3; a sawtooth's 3rd harmonic is 1/3 of the fundamental's amplitude.

definition: A signal that repeats exactly after a fixed time, its period. Steady notes are periodic; noise is not.
example: A 220 Hz sawtooth repeats every 1/220 s, about 4.55 ms.

definition: Describes frequency components that are not whole-number multiples of a sound's fundamental. They sound metallic or clangy; aliasing produces them.
example: An alias at 480 Hz under a 1760 Hz note is inharmonic.

definition: The quality that makes two sounds of the same pitch and loudness sound different, such as a flute and a violin on the same note. It depends largely on the harmonic content and how it changes over time.
example: A sine and a sawtooth at 220 Hz have the same pitch but very different timbres.

definition: A wave that ramps steadily in one direction and then jumps back, once per cycle. It contains every harmonic, each with amplitude 1/k for harmonic k, which makes it bright and a favourite starting point for subtractive synthesis.
example: A 220 Hz sawtooth's 3rd harmonic, at 660 Hz, has a third of the fundamental's amplitude.

definition: A wave that switches between two levels, spending equal time at each. It contains only odd harmonics, with amplitude 1/k for harmonic k, and has the lowest possible crest factor (1).
example: A 3 kHz square wave has harmonics at 3, 9, 15, 21 kHz and so on.

definition: A wave that ramps up and down in straight lines. It has corners but no jumps, so its odd harmonics fall off much faster (as 1/k² for harmonic k) than a square's, and it sounds softer and aliases far less.
example: A triangle's 3rd harmonic is 1/9 of the fundamental's amplitude.

definition: A wave that switches between two levels but, unlike a square, can spend unequal time at each (its duty cycle). Like a square, it has jumps, so it is rich in harmonics and aliases when generated naively.
example: A pulse that is high for 25% of each cycle sounds thinner than a square wave.

definition: The part of a synth that generates a repeating waveform at a set frequency. In software it is usually a phase accumulator followed by a waveform calculation or table lookup.
example: A synth voice might use two detuned sawtooth oscillators.

definition: One number in a digital audio signal: the signal's value measured (or calculated) at one instant. A digital signal is a list of samples taken at a fixed rate.
example: One second of mono audio at 48 kHz is 48,000 samples.

definition: How many samples per second a digital audio signal has, written fs and quoted in hertz. It sets the highest frequency the signal can represent (half the sample rate) and the time available to compute each block.
example: 48 kHz, the usual rate for audio hardware, is 48,000 samples per second.

definition: The time between one sample and the next: one divided by the sample rate.
example: At 48 kHz the sample period is about 20.8 µs.

definition: The whole number n that counts samples from 0. Sample n happens at time n divided by the sample rate. Written x[n] for "the value of sample n".
example: At 48 kHz, sample index 48,000 is exactly one second in.

definition: How many samples describe one cycle of a wave: the sample rate divided by the frequency. It is rarely a whole number.
example: A 440 Hz cycle at 48 kHz spans about 109.09 samples.

definition: How far an oscillator's phase moves on each sample: the frequency divided by the sample rate, in cycles (multiply by 2π for radians). Changing it changes the pitch.
example: 440 Hz at 48 kHz needs a phase increment of about 0.009167 cycles per sample.

definition: A running phase variable that an oscillator increases by the phase increment every sample and wraps back into range (for example 0 to 1) after each cycle. It keeps the phase continuous when the frequency changes.
example: Adding 0.009167 per sample and subtracting 1 whenever the phase reaches 1 produces a steady 440 Hz at 48 kHz.

definition: Bringing a phase back into its range after it completes a cycle, by subtracting one full cycle (1.0, or 2π in radians). It keeps the number small so it never loses precision.
example: A phase of 1.004 wraps to 0.004.

definition: A digital oscillator built from a phase accumulator and a lookup of the waveform for each phase value. Its frequency is set by a number, the phase increment.
example: A synth's software oscillator is essentially an NCO running at the audio sample rate.

definition: A fixed number of samples that audio software processes in one go, for example 48, 64 or 128. The block size divided by the sample rate is how long the hardware takes to play it, and so the deadline for computing the next one.
example: A 128-sample block at 48 kHz lasts about 2.67 ms.

definition: A function the audio system calls each time it needs the next block of samples. It must always finish in less time than the block lasts, or the output runs dry.
example: At 128 samples and 48 kHz, the audio callback runs 375 times a second.

definition: What happens when audio software fails to deliver the next block in time: the hardware has nothing to play, and you hear a click, gap or crackle.
example: If a 2.67 ms block takes 3 ms to compute, the output underruns.

definition: The time available to compute each block of audio: the block's duration. All the work must fit inside it every time, not just on average.
example: At 48 samples and 48 kHz the time budget is 1 ms per block.

definition: A short, sharp unwanted sound caused by a sudden jump in the waveform, for example from a phase reset, a missed block or a signal starting mid-cycle.
example: Resetting an oscillator's phase every 48-sample block at 48 kHz produces a 1 kHz buzz of clicks.

definition: A short burst of change in a signal, such as the attack of a drum hit or a sudden step. Abrupt changes in level, pitch or phase create transients that can be heard as clicks.
example: Changing an oscillator's frequency instantly keeps the output continuous but can still cause a small transient.

definition: A regular, small wobble of pitch, usually a few hertz in rate. In a synth it is made by modulating the oscillator frequency with an LFO.
example: A gentle synth vibrato might swing the pitch ±20 cents at about 5 Hz.

definition: A smooth shift of a note's pitch, usually from a wheel or lever. In MIDI, pitch bend messages are normally interpreted as a number of semitones up to the "bend range", often ±2 semitones.
example: With a ±2 semitone range, a wheel at half its upward travel raises the pitch by 1 semitone.

definition: A smooth slide in pitch from one note to the next instead of an instant jump. In code it means ramping the phase increment while the phase stays continuous.
example: A 50 ms glide from 440 Hz to 880 Hz slides up an octave.

definition: The frequency of a signal at one instant, defined as the rate at which its phase (in cycles) is changing. For a phase accumulator it is exactly the frequency that set the increment.
example: Computing sin(2π·f(t)·t) during a glide gives an instantaneous frequency of f(t) + t·f′(t), not f(t).

definition: In calculus, how fast a quantity is changing at an instant, written for example dφ/dt for the rate of change of φ with time. The product rule gives the derivative of a product of two changing quantities.
example: If phase grows at 440 cycles per second, its derivative is 440 Hz.

definition: A calculus rule: the rate of change of a product u × v is u times the rate of change of v plus v times the rate of change of u.
example: The rate of change of f(t) × t is f(t) + t × f′(t).

definition: The small raised number in 2^x, saying how many copies of the base to multiply together; fractional and negative exponents are allowed. In a floating-point number, the exponent is the field that scales the significand by a power of 2.
Describes growth by repeated multiplication rather than addition, as in 2^x: each fixed step in x multiplies the result by the same factor. Pitch is exponential in frequency: each octave doubles it.
example: Each extra volt in a 1 V/octave synth doubles the frequency, an exponential law.

definition: The inverse of raising to a power: log_b(x) answers "b to what power gives x?". Base 10 (log10) is used for decibels; base 2 (log2) counts octaves.
example: log10(100) = 2 because 10² = 100.

definition: The logarithm that counts doublings: log2(x) is the power you raise 2 to in order to get x. In audio it converts a frequency ratio into octaves.
example: log2(8) = 3, and log2(880/440) = 1 octave.

definition: The logarithm to base e (about 2.718), available in every maths library. Any other logarithm can be computed from it: log2(x) = ln(x) / ln(2).
The rule that a logarithm in any base can be computed from logarithms in another base by division: log_b(x) = ln(x) / ln(b).
A scale where equal steps mean equal multiplications rather than equal additions. Pitch and loudness are both perceived roughly logarithmically, which is why audio uses octaves and decibels.
example: 110 → 220 Hz and 440 → 880 Hz are equal steps on a logarithmic (pitch) scale.

definition: The middle value of two numbers on a multiplicative scale: the square root of their product. Halfway in pitch between two frequencies is their geometric mean.
example: The geometric mean of 220 Hz and 880 Hz is √(220 × 880) = 440 Hz.

definition: The ordinary average: add the values and divide by how many there are.
example: The arithmetic mean of 220 and 880 is 550, which is not halfway in pitch.

definition: The number that, multiplied by itself, gives the original: √x × √x = x. In audio it appears in RMS calculations and in the √2 ratio between a sine's peak and RMS.
The size of a number ignoring its sign, written |x|. The absolute value of −0.7 is 0.7. Peak level uses the largest absolute sample value.
The Greek capital letter Σ (sigma), meaning "add up all of the following" over a range of values.
example: Σ x[n]² over all samples is the total of the squared samples.

definition: The symbol ≈, meaning "approximately equal to": the two sides are equal after rounding or under an approximation.
Two quantities are proportional when one is always a fixed multiple of the other, so if one doubles, so does the other. In formulas it is written with the symbol ∝.
example: Power ∝ amplitude squared, so doubling the amplitude quadruples the power.

definition: The Greek capital letter Δ (delta), usually meaning "a step in" or "a change in" a quantity, such as Δf for the spacing between FFT bins or Δ for a quantisation step.
example: With 1 s of audio at 48 kHz, the FFT bin spacing Δf is 1 Hz.

definition: The remainder after dividing by a number and removing every whole multiple of it. It wraps values into a fixed range, which is how both phase wrapping and alias folding work.
The functions that return the smaller (min) or larger (max) of their inputs. Combined, they clamp a value into a range.
example: min(max(1.7, −1), 1) = 1: a hard clip.

definition: The largest number that divides exactly into all of a set of numbers. The common repetition rate of a set of harmonics is their greatest common divisor.
example: The greatest common divisor of 440, 660 and 880 Hz is 220 Hz.

definition: A number that can't be written as a ratio of two whole numbers, so its decimal expansion never ends or repeats.
example: The 12-TET semitone ratio 2^(1/12) ≈ 1.059463… is irrational.

definition: How high or low a note sounds: a perception, not a physical quantity. For a steady periodic tone it closely tracks the fundamental frequency, and we hear it on a ratio (logarithmic) scale.
example: 440 Hz and 880 Hz have the same pitch class (A), an octave apart.

definition: The musical interval between two notes whose frequencies are in the ratio 2:1. It is 12 semitones, or 1200 cents.
example: 220 Hz to 440 Hz is one octave; 440 Hz to 880 Hz is the next.

definition: The smallest step in Western music, one twelfth of an octave. In 12-TET each semitone multiplies the frequency by 2^(1/12) ≈ 1.0595, and it is 100 cents.
example: One semitone above 440 Hz is about 466.16 Hz.

definition: The distance in pitch between two notes, defined by the ratio of their frequencies and named by its size: octave, fifth, major third and so on.
example: A fifth is 7 semitones; in 12-TET its frequency ratio is about 1.4983.

definition: The tuning system used by almost all synths and pianos: the octave is split into 12 equal semitones, each a frequency ratio of the twelfth root of 2. Every key is equally in tune, at the cost of slightly impure fifths and thirds.
example: The 12-TET fifth is 700 cents; the pure 3:2 fifth is about 701.96 cents.

definition: Tuning intervals to simple whole-number frequency ratios, such as 3:2 for a fifth and 5:4 for a major third, which come from the harmonic series. 12-TET approximates these ratios.
example: A just major third (5:4) is about 13.69 cents narrower than the 12-TET major third.

definition: The musical interval of 7 semitones. Its pure (just) form is the frequency ratio 3:2; in 12-TET it is 2^(7/12) ≈ 1.4983, about 1.96 cents flat of pure.
example: A fifth above 440 Hz is about 659.26 Hz in 12-TET.

definition: The musical interval of 4 semitones. Its pure (just) form is the ratio 5:4; the 12-TET major third, 2^(4/12) ≈ 1.2599, is about 13.69 cents sharp of pure.
example: C♯5 (554.37 Hz) is a 12-TET major third above A4.

definition: A chord of three notes stacked in thirds. A major triad is a root, a major third above it and a fifth above the root.
example: An A major triad from A3 is about 220, 277.18 and 329.63 Hz.

definition: In note names, ♯ (sharp) raises a note by a semitone and ♭ (flat) lowers it. In tuning, "sharp" and "flat" also mean slightly too high or too low in pitch.
example: G♯4 is a semitone above G4; a note 5 cents sharp is 5 cents too high.

definition: A unit of musical interval: one hundredth of a 12-TET semitone, so 1200 cents make an octave. The interval between two frequencies is 1200 × log2(f2 / f1) cents.
example: 445 Hz is about 19.6 cents above 440 Hz.

definition: A small deliberate offset in pitch between oscillators or voices, usually set in cents. Detuned oscillators beat against each other, thickening the sound.
example: Two sawtooths at 220 Hz, one detuned by +7 cents, beat at about 0.89 Hz.

definition: A slow, regular rise and fall in loudness when two tones of nearly the same frequency are combined. They drift in and out of phase, and the wobble rate equals the difference between their frequencies.
example: 440 Hz and 442.55 Hz together beat about 2.55 times a second.

definition: The smallest change in a stimulus, such as pitch, that a listener can reliably detect. For sine tones one commonly cited summary gives about 3 Hz below 500 Hz and about 0.6% (roughly 10 cents) above 1 kHz; it varies with frequency, level and listener.
example: One commonly cited summary gives about 3 Hz for sine tones below 500 Hz.

definition: Musical Instrument Digital Interface: the standard protocol (since 1983) for sending note, controller and timing messages between instruments, controllers and computers. It sends instructions such as "play note 60", not audio.
example: Pressing middle C on a MIDI keyboard sends a Note On message for note number 60.

definition: MIDI's number for a pitch, from 0 to 127, one step per semitone. Note 60 is middle C and note 69 is the A above it, conventionally 440 Hz.
example: Note 72 is an octave above middle C, about 523.25 Hz.

definition: A part of the MIDI specification, agreed by the MIDI Manufacturers Association, with messages that retune notes precisely: a bulk dump giving a tuning for all 128 notes, and a message for retuning individual notes as they play. The Wikipedia article on it gives the standard conversion between note number and frequency in 12-TET with A4 at 440 Hz.
The C nearest the middle of a piano keyboard, about 261.63 Hz in standard tuning. It is MIDI note 60 and is called C4 in scientific pitch notation (though some software calls it C3).
example: Middle C is 9 semitones below A4 (440 Hz).

definition: The A above middle C, MIDI note 69, tuned to 440 Hz by the usual convention (concert pitch). It is the reference note for converting note numbers to frequencies.
example: Changing the reference from 440 Hz to 442 Hz retunes every note by about 7.85 cents.

definition: Naming notes by letter plus octave number, with the octave number going up at each C. Middle C is C4 and the A above it is A4; MIDI note 0 is C−1. Some software (Ableton Live, for example) labels everything an octave lower.
example: The piano's lowest key is A0 (27.5 Hz) and its highest is C8 (about 4186 Hz).

definition: A standard piano has 88 keys, from A0 (27.5 Hz) to C8 (about 4186 Hz): MIDI notes 21 to 108.
example: MIDI note 21 is the piano's lowest A.

definition: A popular digital audio workstation (DAW). By default it labels MIDI note 60 (middle C) as "C3", an octave lower than scientific pitch notation, the same convention Yamaha uses.
example: Note 60 shows as C3 in Ableton Live but C4 in many other programs.

definition: A synth control that changes the reference frequency for A4 (normally 440 Hz), retuning every note by the same ratio.
example: Setting master tune to 415 Hz shifts everything down almost exactly a semitone.

definition: Working with pitch as a (possibly fractional) note number in semitones, where transposing, bending and detuning are simple additions, and converting to hertz only at the end.
example: Note 69 plus a 1-semitone bend plus 15 cents of detune is note 70.15 in note space.

definition: To shift notes up or down by a fixed musical interval. In note space it is adding a number of semitones; in hertz it is multiplying by a ratio.
example: Transposing up an octave adds 12 to every note number and doubles every frequency.

definition: A device or program that measures the frequency of a note and shows the nearest note name and how many cents sharp or flat it is.
example: A tuner reading 415 Hz shows G♯4, about 1.3 cents flat.

definition: An oscillator running below the audio range (typically under about 20 Hz) that is used to modulate another parameter, such as pitch for vibrato, rather than being heard directly.
example: An LFO at 5 Hz swinging the pitch by ±20 cents gives vibrato.

definition: Changing one parameter of a sound over time using another signal, such as an LFO or envelope. Pitch can be modulated linearly (in hertz) or exponentially (in cents or semitones).
example: Exponential pitch modulation of ±39 cents sounds equally deep on every note.

definition: The common analogue-synth control standard, popularised by Moog, in which each extra volt of control voltage raises the pitch one octave (and 1/12 V a semitone). An exponential converter inside the oscillator turns the voltage into frequency.
example: An oscillator at 110 Hz with 0 V plays 440 Hz with 2 V.

definition: In analogue and modular synths, a voltage used to set a parameter such as pitch or filter cut-off, rather than to carry audio.
example: With 1 V/oct, a control voltage rising by 1 V raises the pitch an octave.

definition: A circuit in an analogue oscillator that converts a control voltage into a frequency exponentially, so equal voltage steps give equal pitch steps.
example: It is why a 1 V/oct oscillator doubles its frequency for every extra volt.

definition: Robert Moog's company and synthesizers, which popularised modular voltage-controlled synthesis and the 1 volt per octave standard in the 1960s.
example: The Minimoog is a classic Moog synthesizer.

definition: Making sounds by starting with a harmonically rich waveform, such as a sawtooth, and filtering harmonics away to shape the timbre.
example: Lowering a low-pass filter's cut-off on a sawtooth makes the sound darker without changing its pitch.

definition: The effect where listeners still hear the pitch of a fundamental frequency that has been removed, because the remaining harmonics are spaced at that frequency and the waveform still repeats at its rate.
example: A sawtooth with its 220 Hz component removed is still heard at 220 Hz.

definition: The opening part of a sound, as it rises from silence. How quickly and how noisily a sound starts is a large part of its timbre.
example: A plucked string has a fast attack; a bowed one is slower.

definition: One independent sound-producing channel in a synth, typically oscillators, filter and amplifier for one note. A synth with 8 voices can play 8 notes at once (8-voice polyphony).
example: A 16-voice polyphonic synth must leave headroom for all 16 voices summing.

definition: Division between whole numbers that discards the fraction. In C-family languages it truncates towards zero (−9/12 gives 0); Python's // floors instead (−9 // 12 gives −1), while its / always gives a float.
example: In C, (60 − 69) / 12 is 0, so every note from 58 to 80 plays 440 Hz.

definition: Measuring a continuous signal at evenly spaced instants, turning it into a list of numbers (samples). The rate of measuring is the sample rate.
example: Sampling a microphone signal at 48 kHz takes 48,000 measurements a second.

definition: A signal that has a value at every instant, like the air pressure at your ear or the voltage on a wire, as opposed to a list of samples.
example: A microphone produces a continuous signal; an ADC turns it into samples.

definition: A signal defined only at separate, evenly spaced instants: a sequence of samples x[0], x[1], x[2] … with nothing defined in between.
example: Every sample of a 48 kHz discrete-time signal is 1/48,000 s after the previous one.

definition: A chip or circuit that turns a stream of digital samples into a continuously varying voltage, which can then drive an amplifier and speaker. A good DAC includes reconstruction filtering so the output is smooth.
example: The PCM5102A is a common audio DAC on maker boards.

definition: A chip or circuit that measures a voltage at regular instants and outputs each measurement as a number: it samples and quantises an analogue signal.
example: An audio interface input uses an ADC with an anti-aliasing filter in front of it.

definition: A general word for an ADC or DAC: the chip that crosses between the analogue and digital worlds.
example: A converter's datasheet lists its dynamic range, typically 95–115 dB for common audio parts.

definition: In hardware, a single chip combining an audio ADC and DAC (coder/decoder), often with amplifiers and filters. (In software, "codec" can instead mean a compression format such as MP3.)
example: An embedded synth board usually has an audio codec that takes samples over I²S and outputs line-level audio.

definition: An external box (often USB) that gives a computer high-quality audio inputs and outputs, with ADCs, DACs and preamplifiers.
example: Plugging a synth's line output into an audio interface lets you record it.

definition: The audio format of the compact disc: 16-bit stereo samples at 44.1 kHz.
example: The CD rate puts the Nyquist frequency at 22.05 kHz, just above the limit of hearing.

definition: Audio equipment and practice for studios, broadcast and live sound. It usually runs at 48 kHz (or multiples) and uses +4 dBu line levels.
example: Most pro audio hardware defaults to a 48 kHz sample rate.

definition: Audio recorded or stored at a higher sample rate or bit depth than CD, such as 96 kHz and 24 bits. The extra rate mostly helps processing rather than audible treble.
example: A 96 kHz, 24-bit recording is commonly called high-resolution.

definition: A binary digit, 0 or 1: the smallest unit of digital information. N bits can represent 2^N different values.
example: 16 bits give 65,536 values.

definition: A group of 8 bits, the usual unit of computer memory. A float32 sample takes 4 bytes.
example: One second of mono float32 audio at 48 kHz is 192,000 bytes.

definition: Units of memory size: in this course a kilobyte (kB) is 1,000 bytes and a megabyte (MB) is 1,000,000 bytes. (Some software uses 1,024 and 1,048,576 instead.)
example: A 2-second float32 delay buffer at 48 kHz needs 384 kB per channel.

definition: How many bits per second a stream carries: sample rate × bits per sample × channels for uncompressed audio. A megabit per second (Mbit/s) is 1,000,000 bit/s.
example: Stereo 24-bit audio at 48 kHz carries 2.304 Mbit/s of audio data.

definition: How many bits store each sample; together with integer-or-float it makes up the sample format (for example 16-bit integer or 32-bit float). It sets how finely each value is recorded and so the quantisation noise floor (about 6 dB per bit); it does not change the frequency range.
example: 16-bit audio has 65,536 levels; 24-bit audio has 16,777,216.

definition: Rounding each sample's exact value to the nearest of a fixed set of levels so it can be stored with a limited number of bits. The rounding error it causes is quantisation error.
example: Quantising to 8 bits rounds every sample to a multiple of 2/256 ≈ 0.0078 in the −1..+1 range.

definition: The gap between neighbouring levels a quantised sample can take, equal to the value of one least significant bit (1 LSB). With full scale from −1 to +1 and N bits it is 2/2^N.
example: At 16 bits the step is about 0.0000305; rounding to the nearest level is never more than half a step out.

definition: The bit in a binary number with the smallest value (the 1s place), at the right-hand end when written out. In audio, one LSB is the smallest step a sample can change by; in serial links and MIDI, "LSB" can also mean the least significant byte of a multi-byte value, and "LSB first" says which end is sent first.
example: In the 8-bit number 0b0000_0101 (5), the LSB is 1; MIDI pitch bend sends its 7-bit LSB before its 7-bit MSB.

definition: The rounding error from quantisation, which behaves like a small random hiss added to a busy signal much bigger than one step. For very quiet or very coarsely quantised signals it becomes distortion instead.
example: At 16 bits, quantisation noise sits about 98 dB below a full-scale sine.

definition: How far quantisation noise sits below the signal, in decibels. For a full-scale sine and an ideal N-bit quantiser it is about 6.02 × N + 1.76 dB.
example: 16 bits give about 98 dB SQNR; 24 bits about 146 dB.

definition: How much stronger a wanted signal is than the background noise, usually in decibels. Higher is better.
example: A converter with 114 dB SNR performs like an ideal converter of about 18.6 bits.

definition: The number of bits an ideal converter would need to match a real converter's measured noise performance: (SNR − 1.76) / 6.02.
example: A 24-bit codec with 114 dB of dynamic range has an ENOB of about 18.6.

definition: The ratio between the largest signal a system can handle and its noise floor, in decibels. Converter datasheets measure it in specific ways, often A-weighted with a −60 dBFS test signal.
example: Datasheet dynamic range for common audio converters is roughly 95–115 dB.

definition: The level of background noise in a system, below which quieter signals are lost. In digital audio it is set by quantisation noise or, in real converters, by analogue noise.
example: A 24-bit converter's noise floor is set by its analogue circuitry, far above the 146 dB theoretical figure.

definition: A standard frequency weighting that reduces low and very high frequencies to roughly match how sensitive hearing is at moderate levels. Datasheets often quote A-weighted noise figures, which look better than unweighted ones.
example: A converter's dynamic range is often specified A-weighted.

definition: The largest value a digital format can hold. In floating-point audio, full scale is ±1.0 by convention; levels are measured relative to it in dBFS.
example: A full-scale sine peaks at exactly 1.0, which is 0 dBFS.

definition: Steady, broadband background noise that sounds like "sss". Well-behaved quantisation noise and dither sound like a faint hiss.
example: Dither trades a little extra hiss for no distortion.

definition: Any unwanted change to a signal's waveform that adds new frequency content, such as harmonics from clipping. It is sometimes added deliberately as an effect.
example: Hard clipping a sine adds strong odd-harmonic distortion.

definition: A tiny amount of random noise (about one quantisation step) added before reducing bit depth, so the rounding error becomes random instead of following the signal. It trades a little hiss for no distortion and lets details below one step survive.
example: Exporting a 32-bit float mix to a 16-bit WAV is the classic place to apply dither.

definition: The most common dither type: noise with a triangular probability distribution, 2 quantisation steps wide from peak to peak. It removes distortion and noise modulation, at the cost of raising the noise floor by about 4.8 dB (three times the noise power of plain rounding).
example: TPDF dither is the usual default when converting to 16 bits.

definition: Filtering quantisation noise (with dither) so more of it lands at frequencies where the ear is less sensitive. Unshaped (plain) dither spreads its noise evenly.
example: Noise-shaped dither can make 16-bit audio sound quieter in its noise than plain dither does.

definition: A known signal, usually a sine at a set frequency and level, used to measure a system. Slightly "odd" frequencies such as 997 Hz avoid repeating the same samples every cycle.
example: A 997 Hz sine at −12 dBFS is a safe, practical test tone.

definition: Driving a signal beyond what a stage or format can represent, so it clips. In a quantiser, values beyond the top or bottom level overload it.
example: A 4-bit quantiser whose top code is 0.875 overloads on a 0.999-amplitude sine.

definition: The manufacturer's technical document for a component or product, such as a chip or board, giving its specifications, recommended circuits and limits. It is the authority for figures such as a converter's dynamic range or a board's output level.
example: The PCM5102A datasheet lists a dynamic range of 112 dB.

definition: A large American semiconductor company whose audio converter chips (such as the PCM5102A DAC and PCM1808 ADC) are common on maker and synth boards.
example: TI publishes datasheets for all its converter chips.

definition: A stereo 24-bit audio ADC chip from Texas Instruments, with a datasheet dynamic range of 99 dB.
example: The PCM1808 is a common low-cost ADC on audio breakout boards.

definition: A stereo audio DAC chip from Texas Instruments that accepts samples over I²S, with a datasheet dynamic range of 112 dB. It is popular on maker audio boards.
example: A Teensy or ESP32 synth can drive a PCM5102A board over I²S.

definition: A flagship 24-bit stereo audio DAC chip from Texas Instruments, specified at around 127–132 dB dynamic range.
example: The PCM1792A shows what a top-end converter chip achieves.

definition: A number format that stores a sign, a significand (the digits) and an exponent (a power of 2 that scales them), so it can hold very large and very small values with the same relative precision.
example: Audio software usually processes samples as floats in which ±1.0 is full scale.

definition: The 32-bit floating-point format: 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits and 23 stored fraction bits plus an implicit leading 1, giving 24 bits of precision. It represents every integer exactly only up to 2^24 = 16,777,216.
example: Much synth DSP code on microcontrollers with a single-precision FPU, such as a Cortex-M4F, uses float32.

definition: The 64-bit floating-point format, with 53 bits of precision. NumPy and soundfile use it by default.
example: sf.read returns float64 samples in ±1.0 unless told otherwise.

definition: The part of a floating-point number that holds its significant digits; the exponent then scales it. float32 has a 24-bit significand (23 bits stored).
example: Because the significand has a fixed number of bits, a float keeps the same relative precision at any size.

definition: A way of storing fractional numbers as integers with an agreed scale factor, so the binary point is in a fixed place. It is common on chips without a floating-point unit and in converter interfaces.
example: A 16-bit fixed-point sample of 16,384 means 0.5 if the scale is 32,768.

definition: A whole number type that can be negative. With N bits it runs from −2^(N−1) to 2^(N−1) − 1, one more negative value than positive. int16 and int32 are the 16- and 32-bit versions.
example: int16 runs from −32,768 to +32,767.

definition: When a calculation produces a value too large for its number type. Integers may wrap round to large values of the opposite sign or behave unpredictably, which in audio sounds like a loud crack.
example: Adding several full-scale int16 voices overflows; in float32 the same sum is fine.

definition: The margin between normal operating level and the maximum a system can handle. In audio it is the gap between a signal's normal peak level and the clipping point (0 dBFS digitally), which leaves room for unexpected peaks.
example: A peak of 0.25 leaves 12 dB of headroom.

definition: Hardware in a processor that does floating-point arithmetic quickly. Microcontrollers without one must emulate floats slowly in software, so they often use fixed-point instead.
example: The Cortex-M4F has a single-precision FPU; the Cortex-M7's optional FPU can be single-precision only or single and double precision, depending on the chip.

definition: A small computer on a single chip, with processor, memory and input/output, used in embedded devices. Synth projects often run their audio code on one, with limited RAM and sometimes no FPU.
example: A microcontroller with a few hundred kB of RAM may not fit a long stereo delay buffer.

definition: A common uncompressed audio file format that stores PCM (or float) samples with a header giving the sample rate, bit depth and channels.
example: A 2-second mono 24-bit WAV at 48 kHz holds 96,000 samples.

definition: The standard way to store uncompressed digital audio: a sequence of quantised integer samples at a fixed rate. In soundfile, PCM_16 and PCM_24 are 16- and 24-bit integer WAV formats.
example: CD audio is 16-bit stereo PCM at 44.1 kHz.

definition: In C and C++, an operation the language standard puts no requirements on, so the program may do anything. Converting a float to an integer type that can't hold its value is undefined behaviour.
example: Casting 1.7 × 32767 to a 16-bit integer in C is undefined behaviour, not a clip.

definition: Converting a value from one number type to another, such as float to integer. A raw cast does not clip out-of-range values; you must clamp first.
example: NumPy's astype(np.int16) on 1.7 × 32767 silently gave −9833 in testing.

definition: The processor family used in most desktop and laptop PCs (Intel and AMD). On x86, an out-of-range float-to-int conversion typically gives the "integer indefinite" value, −2,147,483,648 for 32 bits.
example: Denormal arithmetic on x86 can cost around 100 extra clock cycles per operation.

definition: The special value x86 processors return when a float can't be converted to the requested integer type: the most negative integer, −2,147,483,648 for 32 bits.
example: An over-range sample converted on x86 can become −2,147,483,648, a full-scale crack.

definition: Compiled programming languages widely used for embedded and real-time audio code. Both leave some operations, such as out-of-range float-to-integer conversion, as undefined behaviour.
example: Most synth firmware is written in C or C++.

definition: Converting a number to an integer by dropping its fractional part, which rounds towards zero. As quantisation it can be wrong by nearly a full step, versus half a step for rounding to the nearest level.
example: Truncating −1.7 gives −1; rounding gives −2.

definition: Replacing a number by the nearest allowed value. Rounding to the nearest quantisation level keeps the error within half a step.
example: Rounding 1.2 × 4 = 4.8 to the nearest integer gives 5.

definition: A constant value added to a signal so that it no longer averages to zero. It wastes headroom and can cause thumps when audio starts or stops. It is the 0 Hz component of the spectrum.
example: A signal whose samples average 0.1 has a DC offset of 0.1.

definition: Current or voltage that stays constant rather than alternating. In audio, "DC" usually means a signal's constant (0 Hz) part.
example: An FFT's bin 0 measures the DC component.

definition: A floating-point value so close to zero that it is stored without the usual implicit leading 1. On some processors arithmetic on them is very slow (around 100 extra clock cycles per operation on x86), which decaying filters and reverbs can trigger.
example: Switching on flush-to-zero mode for the audio thread avoids denormal slowdowns.

definition: Processor modes that treat denormal results (FTZ) and inputs (DAZ) as zero, avoiding their slow handling. Audio frameworks often enable them for the audio thread.
example: With FTZ on, a reverb tail decays to exact zero instead of slowing the CPU.

definition: One tick of a processor's clock, the basic unit of time for its operations.
example: An operation on a denormal can take around 100 extra clock cycles on x86.

definition: The thread in an audio program that computes the samples, usually at high priority and with a strict deadline every block. It must avoid slow or unpredictable operations.
example: Memory allocation and file access are avoided on the audio thread.

definition: Mono audio has one channel; stereo has two (left and right), each with its own stream of samples. Memory and data rates scale with the number of channels.
example: A stereo delay needs twice the buffer memory of a mono one.

definition: Inter-IC Sound: a simple serial bus for sending audio samples between chips, such as from a microcontroller to a DAC. It uses a bit clock, a word (left/right) clock and a data line.
example: Stereo 24-bit audio at 48 kHz in 32-bit I²S slots needs a 3.072 MHz bit clock.

definition: A clock signal that ticks once per data bit, so the receiver knows when to read each bit. In I²S it is the BCLK line, whose rate is sample rate × bits per slot × channels.
The fixed-length space for one channel's sample in each I²S frame. 24-bit samples often travel in 32-bit slots, with the spare bits padded.
example: Two 32-bit slots per frame carry one stereo sample pair.

definition: An effect that stores audio in a buffer and plays it back later, producing echoes. The longest delay sets how much memory the buffer needs.
example: A 1.5-second stereo float32 delay at 48 kHz needs 576 kB.

definition: An effect (or the natural acoustic phenomenon) of many dense, decaying reflections that make a sound seem to be in a space.
example: A long reverb tail decays towards zero and can produce denormals.

definition: The result that a signal containing only frequencies below B can be reconstructed exactly from samples taken at a rate greater than 2B. Turned around: a sample rate can represent frequencies only below half of itself.
example: At 48 kHz, any signal entirely below 24 kHz is captured perfectly.

definition: Half the sample rate: the boundary below which frequencies are represented exactly and above which they alias. Signals must stay strictly below it.
example: The Nyquist frequency of 44.1 kHz audio is 22.05 kHz.

definition: The range of frequencies a signal contains. A band-limited signal has nothing above some frequency; ideal sawtooth and square waves are not band-limited because their harmonics go on forever.
example: A sine at 10 kHz is band-limited to 10 kHz and samples perfectly at 48 kHz.

definition: What happens when a frequency above the Nyquist frequency is sampled: it produces exactly the same samples as a lower frequency (its alias) and appears there instead, usually as an inharmonic, out-of-tune tone that can't be removed afterwards.
example: At 48 kHz, a 30 kHz tone aliases to 18 kHz.

definition: The way frequencies above Nyquist map back into the range 0 to Nyquist, like a paper fan creased at every multiple of half the sample rate. As a true frequency rises past Nyquist, its alias falls.
example: At 48 kHz, 26 kHz folds back to 22 kHz.

definition: Flipping a signal upside down (multiplying every sample by −1). For a sine it is the same as a half-cycle phase shift.
example: A 30 kHz sine sampled at 48 kHz gives the 18 kHz samples with their sign flipped.

definition: Above the range of human hearing, roughly above 20 kHz.
example: DAC images around 48 kHz are ultrasonic but can still upset downstream equipment.

definition: A waveform generated directly from its ideal mathematical shape, for example a sawtooth computed straight from the phase. Its jumps contain harmonics above Nyquist, which alias.
example: A naive 1760 Hz sawtooth at 48 kHz has an alias at 480 Hz only about 29 dB down.

definition: How quickly a level falls with frequency: the drop in dB for each doubling of frequency. Harmonics falling as 1/k drop 6 dB per octave; as 1/k², 12 dB per octave.
example: A sawtooth's harmonics fall at 6 dB per octave.

definition: A filter that lets frequencies below its cut-off through and progressively reduces those above. It removes content above Nyquist before sampling and images after conversion; in a synth it darkens bright waveforms.
example: Turning a low-pass cut-off down from 5 kHz to 500 Hz removes most of a sawtooth's upper harmonics.

definition: The frequency at which a filter starts to reduce the signal significantly, conventionally where the output is 3 dB down.
example: A resonant filter boosts frequencies near its cut-off.

definition: A filter computed on samples by arithmetic rather than built from components. It can be very steep, and is used inside converters and for oversampling.
example: A delta-sigma ADC uses a steep digital filter before reducing its rate to 48 kHz.

definition: A low-pass filter placed before sampling to remove content above the Nyquist frequency, so that it cannot fold back into the audio band.
example: Every audio interface input has an anti-aliasing filter in front of its ADC.

definition: The range of frequencies between where a filter passes the signal and where it fully blocks it. Real filters need one.
example: CD's 44.1 kHz rate leaves a transition band between 20 kHz and 22.05 kHz.

definition: The passband is the range of frequencies a filter lets through; the stopband is the range it blocks.
example: An alias at 800 Hz is in the downsampling filter's passband, so it survives.

definition: The design used by most modern audio converters: it runs at many times the final sample rate with very few bits and uses digital filtering, so only a simple analogue filter is needed outside.
example: A delta-sigma ADC samples far faster than 48 kHz, then filters and reduces the rate digitally.

definition: Running processing at a multiple of the output sample rate (for example 4×), so harmonics have more room before they alias, then low-pass filtering and downsampling. It reduces aliasing but doesn't remove it.
example: 2× oversampling a naive 1760 Hz saw lowers its worst in-band aliases by roughly 10 dB.

definition: Reducing the sample rate by low-pass filtering below the new Nyquist frequency and then keeping only every Nth sample.
example: Downsampling from 96 kHz to 48 kHz keeps every second sample after filtering.

definition: Building a sound by adding sine waves, one per harmonic. For an alias-free oscillator you simply stop adding below Nyquist, but it is costly for low notes with hundreds of harmonics.
example: A band-limited sawtooth at 110 Hz needs about 200 sines below 22 kHz.

definition: A stored single cycle of a waveform containing only harmonics that fit below Nyquist for a given pitch range. Several tables cover different ranges, and the oscillator picks one per note.
example: A high note uses a table with fewer harmonics than a low note.

definition: An alias-reducing technique that builds classic waveforms from a band-limited train of impulses, described by Stilson and Smith.
example: Integrating a BLIT produces a band-limited sawtooth.

definition: An alias-reducing technique, described by Eli Brandt (2001), that generates a waveform naively and then smooths each jump with a precomputed band-limited correction.
example: Adding a BLEP at each sawtooth reset removes most of its aliasing.

definition: A cheap approximation of BLEP, introduced by Välimäki and Huovilainen (2007), that uses a short polynomial correction around each discontinuity instead of a stored table. It is light enough for small processors.
example: A PolyBLEP sawtooth costs only a few extra operations per sample.

definition: Processing whose output is not simply proportional to its input, such as clipping, distortion and waveshaping. It creates new harmonics, which can alias. Gain, mixing and linear filters are linear and create none.
example: Hard-clipping a 5 kHz sine creates harmonics at 15, 25, 35 kHz and so on.

definition: Distorting a signal by passing each sample through a fixed curve (a transfer function), such as tanh. It creates new harmonics.
example: A tanh waveshaper is a common soft clipper.

definition: Frequency modulation: making sounds by rapidly varying one oscillator's frequency with another, which creates many sidebands (new frequency components). Those above Nyquist can alias.
example: The Yamaha DX7 popularised FM synthesis.

definition: A simple way of turning samples into a voltage by holding each value until the next, giving a staircase. Its output contains images and is slightly rolled off (a sinc-shaped response).
example: A 1 kHz tone through a zero-order hold at 48 kHz still has images near 47 and 49 kHz.

definition: Copies of a sampled signal's spectrum that appear around every multiple of the sample rate when samples are turned back into a voltage. A reconstruction filter removes them.
example: A 1 kHz tone at 48 kHz has images at 47, 49, 95 and 97 kHz.

definition: The low-pass filter after a DAC that removes the images above the audio band, leaving the smooth signal the sampling theorem promises.
example: Follow the codec datasheet's recommended output circuit for the reconstruction filter.

definition: The function sin(x)/x. It describes the ideal reconstruction of a sampled signal and the frequency response of a zero-order hold.
example: A zero-order hold's response falls off as a sinc shape, weakening but not removing images.

definition: A description of how much of each frequency a signal contains, usually plotted as level against frequency. An FFT computes it from samples.
example: A sawtooth's spectrum shows peaks at every harmonic.

definition: Processing where the output is proportional to the input and sums of inputs give sums of outputs, such as gain, mixing and ordinary filters. It changes levels of existing frequencies but creates no new ones.
example: Multiplying a 5 kHz sine by 0.5 is linear: the output is still only 5 kHz.

definition: A logarithmic unit for ratios. For amplitudes it is 20 × log10(ratio); for powers, 10 × log10(ratio). A decibel always compares with a reference; suffixes such as dBFS, dBu and dBV name the reference.
example: Doubling an amplitude is +6.02 dB; halving it is −6.02 dB.

definition: In signal terms, the average of the squared amplitude (mean square), proportional to physical power. Unrelated signals add in power, not amplitude.
example: Four equal unrelated sources have four times the power of one, +6 dB.

definition: Decibels relative to full scale: the level of a digital signal compared with the largest value the format can hold. 0 dBFS is the maximum, so normal levels are negative. RMS readings in dBFS follow different conventions.
example: A peak of 0.25 is about −12 dBFS.

definition: The largest absolute sample value (or voltage) in a signal. It decides whether a signal will clip.
example: A sine of amplitude 0.8 has a peak level of 0.8, about −1.9 dBFS.

definition: The square root of the average of the squared samples: a measure of a signal's average size that tracks its power and relates more closely to loudness than peak level does. For a sine it is the peak divided by √2.
example: A sine peaking at 0.5 has an RMS of about 0.354.

definition: A signal's peak divided by its RMS, often in dB. It says how far peaks stand above the average level: 1 (0 dB) for a square wave, √2 (3.01 dB) for a sine, and typically 12–20 dB for real music.
example: A peak of 1.9 with an RMS of 0.35 is a crest factor of about 14.7 dB.

definition: The distance from a waveform's lowest point to its highest. For a symmetric wave it is twice the peak.
example: A sine at 1.228 V RMS is about 3.47 V peak-to-peak.

definition: AES17 is the Audio Engineering Society's standard for measuring digital audio equipment. It defines the RMS level of a full-scale sine as 0 dBFS, so a full-scale square reads +3 dBFS.
example: A meter following AES17 reads a full-scale sine as 0 dBFS RMS.

definition: The International Electrotechnical Commission, which publishes international standards for electrical and electronic equipment, including audio measurement.
example: IEC standards cover how audio levels and meters are specified.

definition: The International Telecommunication Union, the United Nations agency for telecommunications standards, including broadcast audio level standards.
example: ITU recommendations define loudness metering for broadcast.

definition: Combining signals by adding them sample by sample, usually after scaling each one. Identical in-phase signals add in amplitude; unrelated ones add in power.
example: Three sines each peaking at 0.8 can sum to a peak of 2.4.

definition: Correlated signals move together (such as identical, in-phase copies), so their amplitudes add. Uncorrelated (unrelated) signals, such as different frequencies or independent noise, add in power on average.
example: Two equal uncorrelated signals give about +3 dB of RMS; two identical in-phase ones give +6 dB.

definition: What happens when a signal exceeds what a stage or format can represent and its peaks are flattened at the limit. Accidental clipping sounds harsh; deliberate clipping is a distortion effect.
example: A sine at amplitude 2.0 clipped to ±1.0 gains strong odd harmonics.

definition: Clipping that flattens anything beyond the limit abruptly, leaving sharp corners. It creates strong high harmonics (odd ones if symmetric) that alias in a digital synth.
example: At 2× overdrive, hard clipping's 9th harmonic is about 20 dB stronger than tanh soft clipping's.

definition: Clipping that bends the waveform gradually towards the limit, for example with tanh. Small signals pass almost unchanged and high harmonics fall away much faster than with hard clipping.
example: A soft clipper before the output turns rare overshoots into mild saturation.

definition: Converting or computing so that out-of-range results stick at the nearest limit instead of wrapping round. Clamping a float to ±1.0 before converting to integers does this.
example: Clamping 1.7 to 1.0 before scaling to int16 gives 32,767 instead of a wrapped value.

definition: A processor that automatically turns the gain down quickly whenever the level would exceed a ceiling, catching peaks without hard clipping.
example: Many polyphonic synths put a limiter before the output to catch rare in-phase peaks.

definition: The property of a waveform whose second half-cycle is the upside-down copy of the first. Such waveforms contain only odd harmonics.
example: A sine clipped equally top and bottom keeps half-wave symmetry, so it gains only odd harmonics.

definition: The factor by which a stage multiplies a signal's amplitude, often given in decibels. Gains in dB add where linear gain factors multiply.
example: A gain of −6 dB multiplies the samples by about 0.501.

definition: Setting the level at each stage of a signal chain so that no stage clips and none is needlessly quiet.
example: In a float synth, gain staging mostly means protecting the final conversion.

definition: A boost a filter applies to frequencies near its cut-off, set by the resonance control. High resonance can raise those frequencies well above the input level, so it needs headroom.
example: Full resonance on a low-pass filter makes it ring at its cut-off frequency.

definition: A control signal that shapes how a parameter changes over a note's life, typically attack, decay, sustain and release (ADSR). The amp envelope shapes loudness.
example: A slow attack on the amp envelope makes a note fade in.

definition: A number from MIDI (1–127 in a Note On) saying how hard a key was struck, commonly used to set a note's loudness or brightness.
example: Rendering every note at maximum velocity tests the worst-case level.

definition: Routing part of an effect's output back to its input, as in delay and reverb. High feedback makes levels build up and needs headroom.
example: A delay with 90% feedback repeats for a long time and can grow louder than its input with other processing in the loop.

definition: A buzzy, stepped artefact heard when a parameter such as gain jumps in coarse steps (for example as a knob is read) instead of changing smoothly.
example: Smoothing a volume knob over a few milliseconds removes zipper noise.

definition: Changing a control value gradually over a short time instead of jumping, to avoid clicks and zipper noise.
example: Ramping a gain change over 10 ms avoids an audible step.

definition: The standard signal level for connecting audio equipment, between mic level and speaker level. Pro gear uses +4 dBu nominal (about 1.228 V RMS); consumer gear −10 dBV (about 0.316 V RMS).
example: A synth's line output plugs into a mixer's or interface's line input.

definition: The typical operating level a piece of equipment is designed around. Real signals peak well above it, so equipment has headroom.
example: +4 dBu is the nominal level for pro line inputs.

definition: Decibels relative to 0.7746 V RMS (the voltage that dissipates 1 mW in 600 Ω). Pro line level is +4 dBu.
Decibels relative to 1 V RMS. Consumer line level is −10 dBV.
example: −10 dBV ≈ 0.316 V RMS.

term: Instrument, mic, headphone and speaker levels
definition: Other standard signal levels, from very small (microphone, a few millivolts) to large (speaker outputs from a power amplifier, tens of volts). They are not interchangeable with line level.
example: Never connect a power amplifier's speaker output to a line input or development board.

definition: An amplifier that raises a line-level signal to the voltage and current needed to drive loudspeakers.
example: A power amplifier's speaker output can carry tens of volts.

definition: A ready-made circuit board carrying a microcontroller (and sometimes an audio codec) with connectors, used to prototype projects such as a synth.
example: A development board's documentation gives its maximum audio output level.

definition: A popular general-purpose programming language. With NumPy, matplotlib and soundfile it is a convenient workbench for generating and measuring audio offline.
example: math.sin in Python takes radians.

definition: The standard Python library for fast arrays and numerical maths, including the FFT (numpy.fft). Audio is handled as an array of samples.
example: np.arange(48000) / 48000 gives one second of sample times at 48 kHz.

definition: The standard Python plotting library, used to draw waveforms and spectra.
example: ax.plot(t, x, marker=".") draws a waveform with each sample marked as a dot.

definition: A Python library, built on libsndfile, for reading and writing audio files such as WAV as NumPy arrays.
example: sf.write("a440.wav", x, 48000, subtype="PCM_24") writes a 24-bit WAV.

definition: A widely used C library for reading and writing audio file formats. soundfile is a Python wrapper around it.
example: In the version tested (1.2.2), libsndfile's clipping conversion rounded down.

definition: soundfile's name for a file's sample encoding: for example PCM_16 and PCM_24 (16- and 24-bit integers) or FLOAT (32-bit float, which keeps values above 1.0).
example: Use subtype="FLOAT" to keep headroom in an analysis file.

definition: NumPy's name for the type of the numbers in an array, such as float64, float32, int16 or int32.
example: sf.read(path, dtype="int16") returns 16-bit integers instead of floats.

definition: A self-contained folder of Python packages for one project, so its library versions don't clash with others and experiments can be reproduced.
example: python3 -m venv .venv creates one; . .venv/bin/activate switches to it.

definition: Python's package installer. pip freeze lists the exact installed versions, which are saved to requirements.txt for reproducibility.
example: pip install numpy matplotlib soundfile installs the measurement toolkit.

definition: A text file listing a Python project's packages and versions, so anyone can recreate the same environment with pip install -r requirements.txt.
example: Commit requirements.txt alongside your experiments.

definition: Special floating-point values: NaN ("not a number") results from undefined operations such as 0/0, and ±infinity from overflow or division by zero. In audio they usually mean a bug such as an unstable filter, and they spread through every calculation they touch.
example: np.isfinite(x).all() is False if any sample is NaN or infinite.

definition: A (usually feedback) filter whose output grows without limit instead of settling, often ending in infinity or NaN. Extreme settings or coefficient bugs can cause it.
example: A filter that blew up shows NaN samples in the render.

definition: Computing audio into a file or array without playing it in real time, so it can be measured and checked by numbers.
example: An offline render of the worst-case patch reveals its true peak level.

definition: Looking at a signal as values over time (the samples themselves), as opposed to the frequency domain, which shows how much of each frequency it contains.
example: Counting zero crossings measures frequency in the time domain.

definition: Looking at a signal as how much of each frequency it contains, usually computed with an FFT.
example: Aliases that are invisible on a waveform plot stand out in the frequency domain.

definition: A point where a signal passes through zero. Upward crossings (from negative to non-negative) happen once per cycle of a clean sine, so their spacing gives the period.
example: 997 Hz at 48 kHz has an upward zero crossing about every 48.14 samples.

definition: An efficient algorithm for computing the discrete Fourier transform: given N samples, it returns how much of each of N evenly spaced frequencies they contain. It is the standard tool for looking at a spectrum.
example: An FFT of 48,000 samples at 48 kHz has bins 1 Hz apart.

definition: The mathematical transform that expresses a block of samples as a sum of sines and cosines at evenly spaced frequencies. The FFT is a fast way to compute it.
example: Julius O. Smith's "Mathematics of the DFT" is a free introduction.

definition: NumPy's FFT for real-valued input. For N samples (N even) it returns N/2 + 1 complex values, for frequencies from 0 Hz to the Nyquist frequency; rfftfreq gives those frequencies.
example: np.fft.rfft of 48,000 samples returns 24,001 values.

definition: One of the evenly spaced frequencies at which an FFT reports a value. Bin k is at k × (sample rate ÷ number of samples).
example: With 10 Hz bins, bin 100 is at 1000 Hz.

definition: The frequency gap between neighbouring FFT bins: the sample rate divided by the number of samples, which is one over the capture's duration. Longer captures give finer spacing.
example: 0.1 s of audio gives 10 Hz bins; 2 s gives 0.5 Hz bins.

definition: The size of a complex FFT value, ignoring its phase (numpy's np.abs). Scaled by 2 divided by the sum of the window, it reads a sine's amplitude.
example: A raw rfft magnitude of 12,000 from 48,000 unwindowed samples means an amplitude of 0.5.

definition: A number with a real and an imaginary part. An FFT returns one per bin, whose size (magnitude) is the amount of that frequency and whose angle is its phase.
example: np.abs of a complex FFT value gives its magnitude.

definition: A smooth curve, zero or small at the ends, multiplied into a capture before an FFT so its abrupt start and end don't smear energy across the spectrum (leakage).
example: Windowing a 1,005 Hz tone with Hann keeps leakage 500 Hz away near −118 dB instead of −52 dB.

definition: A popular window shaped like one raised cosine cycle: 0.5 − 0.5 × cos(2πn/(N − 1)). It is a good default for audio spectra, with low far-off leakage.
example: Between bins, a Hann window loses about 1.42 dB at the peak.

definition: Using no window at all, which is the same as multiplying by 1 inside the capture and 0 outside. Its spectrum has high, slowly decaying sidelobes, so it leaks badly between bins.
example: Between bins, an unwindowed (rectangular) capture loses about 3.92 dB at the peak.

definition: The smearing of a frequency's energy into many FFT bins when it does not fit a whole number of cycles in the capture. Windowing greatly reduces it.
example: Unwindowed, a 1,005 Hz tone in 10 Hz bins leaks to −52 dB as far as 500 Hz away.

definition: In a window's spectrum, the main lobe is the central peak a tone spreads into and the sidelobes are the smaller ripples either side. Low sidelobes mean little leakage; a narrow main lobe means sharp frequency resolution.
example: A Hann window's sidelobes fall away much faster than a rectangular window's.

definition: The drop in an FFT's peak reading when a tone falls between bins instead of on one. It is worst halfway between bins.
example: Halfway between bins: about 1.42 dB for Hann, about 3.92 dB with no window.

definition: A window designed to read amplitudes accurately even between bins, at the cost of a wider peak.
example: Use a flat-top window when you need the exact level of a tone that isn't on a bin.

definition: Choosing a test frequency so that a whole number of cycles fits in the capture, which puts it exactly on an FFT bin and avoids leakage and scalloping.
example: At 48 kHz with 4,800 samples, 1000 Hz (100 cycles) is coherently sampled; 1005 Hz is not.

definition: Appending zeros to a capture before an FFT. It interpolates the spectrum's shape but adds no information, so it cannot separate close frequencies.
example: Zero-padding 1 s of audio to 2 s doesn't give true 0.5 Hz resolution.

definition: A gradual change of gain at the start or end of a sound, so it doesn't begin or end with a jump (which clicks).
example: A 10 ms fade at each end of a test file prevents clicks.

definition: Software for recording, editing and mixing audio and MIDI, such as Ableton Live, Logic or Reaper.
example: Import a 24-bit WAV into a DAW to listen to a test render.

definition: The playback volume of your speakers or headphones (monitors). Keep it low before playing anything untested, then raise it gradually.
example: A full-scale test sine at a high monitor level is fatiguing and can damage hearing.

definition: Reading a file (or converted data) back in and comparing it with what you wrote, to confirm the format, length and error are as intended.
example: A 24-bit WAV read back differed from the original by at most one 24-bit step.

definition: A number you multiply by to convert between two scales. In digital audio it converts between floats in ±1.0 and integers, such as 32,767 or 32,768 for 16 bits; using different factors for the two directions shrinks the signal on each round trip.
example: Multiplying by 32,767 then dividing by 32,768 turns 1.0 into 0.99997.

definition: A bug where a count is one too many or too few, such as a loop that drops the last partial block of audio.
example: A 1 s render at 48 kHz with 47,952 samples has lost a 48-sample block.
